video_caption: The video segment begins with the title card displaying "A Touch of Venus" in elegant white font on a black background, with a logo in the upper right corner that shows a white outline of a person hugging a globe-like object filled with stars; the logo also includes the text "A Touch of the Universe". A voice over notes that this is a tutorial on how to use the "A Touch of Venus" kit, and notes it is part of a larger project called "A Touch of the Universe." A website view of "A Touch of the Universe" then appears with similar text, logo, and menu items "Home," "Project," "Team," "Downloads," "Tutorials," "Gallery," and "Contact," along with language options "Español" and "Italiano". The website explains in text that "A Touch of the Universe" is a nonprofit project for a tactile astronomy kit for children with vision impairments, adding that an extension including a 3D tactile Venus globe along with an activity book and video tutorials is in development. Below the explanation is the same text and logo as the title card, and at the bottom of the screen a URL appears: "https://astrokit.uv.es"

This video segment shows an educational kit provided by the International Astronomical Union's Office of Astronomy for Development. It begins with the OAD logo, which is rendered against a black background as a white square. The logo depicts the letters "OAD" in white against a black circle, surrounded by concentric dotted circles of different colors, and is accompanied by the words "INTERNATIONAL ASTRONOMICAL UNION" and "OFFICE OF ASTRONOMY FOR DEVELOPMENT". The scene transitions to a beige table, where we see a yellow-and-brown Venus tactile globe; a presentation letter; "A Touch of Venus" activity book, with the title in English and the names of the authors, also in English; an annotated map; and a dark-blue tote bag with a white design of a person standing in a landscape and looking at the sky. The contents of the kit are displayed to show educational materials accessible to both the general public and the blind or visually impaired.

The video segment features a table covered with a white piece of paper, on the right of which reads, "A Touch of Venus is funded by the IAU Office of Astronomy for Development (OAD). All materials have been produced under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)," indicating the materials are created with the support of the IAU for educational purposes, under a specific creative commons license. A white ribbon with red floral pattern is centered on the table. It is spaced at every seven centimeters to measure the distances on the globe by touch. The scene then transitions to reveal a dark blue tote bag displaying a white illustration of a person reaching towards a celestial object surrounded by stars. The text beneath the illustration reads "A Touch of the Universe." Below it are logos for OAD (Office of Astronomy for Development), the Observatori Astronomic Universitat De Valencia (Astronomical Observatory of the University of Valencia), and the Universitat de Valencia (University of Valencia), suggesting the bag is associated with educational outreach or astronomy projects at the University of Valencia. A document is also on the table, which reads, "A Touch Of Venus. Venus Model with feature names. Venus Model with feature projects."

This video segment features an overview of educational materials. On a light wooden table, the items are carefully arranged against a plain wall. The objects include a textured model of a planetary object, possibly Jupiter, mounted on a blue base. Adjacent to the model, there are two books, "A Touch of the Universe: Guide for Visually Impaired People (Guía para personas con discapacidad visual)" and "A Touch of the Universe: Guide for Sighted People (Guía para personas videntes)," referring to guides designed for differently-abled individuals. Nearby, there is a blue tote bag with a print of constellations and the text "A Touch of the Universe" along with organizational logos, suggesting a science outreach program. A printed document and a ribbon are also visible on the table. Throughout the video, the camera remains static, providing a clear view of the materials. Near the end of the video segment, the camera pans in on the planetary object. The URL "https://astrokit.uv.es" is overlaid on the screen, offering access to more information about the project.

The video segment shows a yellow, textured globe-like object, which is a tactile model of Venus sitting on a light-colored table against a muted blue background. The model has a line running from top to bottom, and a small circle attached at the top. A book appears, titled "1. EXPLORING THE TACTILE VENUS MODEL." The book details the objective, which is to familiarize participants with the Venus tactile model, along with the suggested age, duration, materials, and activity description. The activity procedure involves presenting the tactile Venus model to participants and demonstrating how to identify the North Pole by locating the smooth shape of one of the polar caps. The description in the video mentions that the model represents Venus and notes the two polar caps, which appear as smooth circles. It also mentions that the north pole is marked by a smooth circle and that the south pole has the logo of the Astronomical Observatory of the University of Valencia. A meridian runs through the poles, corresponding to the geographic 0° longitude on Venus. These elements are meant to serve as reference points for exploring Venus.

The video segment showcases a tactile model of Venus along with an associated activity book, aimed at teaching geography to children, in an indoor educational setting. At the beginning of the video, a person is seen pointing out features on the Venus model, specifically in the Aphrodite Terra region. The segment then transitions to an open activity book with text in English, listing facts and figures about Venus, its mythological associations, and names of craters. The text includes names like Aphrodite, Ishtar, Lada, Guinevere, Sedna, Tinatin, Cleopatra, Irène Joliot-Curie, Maria Yermolova, Valentina Aleksandrovna Fedorets, Rosa Bonheur and Atalanta. The book provides background information on the women who gave their names to geological formations on Venus. Later, the person is seen demonstrating how to find the French physicist Irène Joliot-Curie crater on the model using a measuring tape and knotting method to find a specific feature along the meridian. The Venus model has an orange-yellow textured surface with some smooth regions. The final part of the video shows the entire set of materials for the activity on the table, including the model, the book, a page of text, and a blue bag with the text "A Touch of the Universe" and the address https://astrokit.uv.es.
